sea50.title: Sentinel Event Alert, Issue 50: Medical device alarm safety in hospitals
sea50.author: The Joint Commission
sea50.quote: The number of alarm signals per patient per day can reach several hundred depending on the unit within the hospital, translating to thousands of alarm signals on every unit and tens of thousands of alarm signals throughout the hospital every day. It is estimated that between 85 and 99 percent of alarm signals do not require clinical intervention... As a result, clinicians become desensitized or immune to the sounds, and are overwhelmed by information - in short, they suffer from "alarm fatigue." In response to this constant barrage of noise, clinicians may turn down the volume of the alarm, turn it off, or adjust the alarm settings outside the limits that are safe and appropriate for the patient - all of which can have serious, often fatal, consequences. ... The Joint Commission's Sentinel Event database* includes reports of 98 alarm-related events between January 2009 and June 2012. Of the 98 reported events, 80 resulted in death, 13 in permanent loss of function, and five in unexpected additional care or extended stay. ... Absent or inadequate alarm system (30) / Improper alarm settings (21) / Alarm signals not audible in all areas (25) / Alarm signals inappropriately turned off (36) ... Alarm fatigue - the most common contributing factor
supports: 85 and 99 percent of alarm signals do not require clinical intervention
several hundred alarm signals per patient per day

Alarm signals inappropriately turned off (36) as the largest single reported contributing factor
alarm fatigue named the most common contributing factor
recommendation 8 asks organisations to assess whether critical alarm signals are audible
sea50.note: Text extracted with pdftotext from the PDF itself, not from an index page. The example case inside SEA 50 is a different incident - a 60-year-old man in the summer of 2010 - and is NOT the Massachusetts General Hospital case. Curly quotes and en-dashes in the source are rendered here as straight quotes and hyphens. The '85 to 99 percent' estimate is carried by SEA 50 but footnoted to AAMI (Horizons, Spring 2011), so the prose attributes it to no one rather than to the Joint Commission. SEA 50 names alarm fatigue 'the most common contributing factor' in a separate list from the four counted factors, which is why the prose says 'reported most often' of the turned-off count (36) rather than calling it the largest factor outright.

globe2011.title: Patient alarms often unheard, unheeded (The Boston Globe, first of two parts)
globe2011.author: Liz Kowalczyk
globe2011.quote: The most widely publicized case was in January 2010 at Massachusetts General Hospital, when an elderly man suffered a fatal heart attack while the crisis alarm on his cardiac monitor was turned off and staff did not respond to numerous lower-level alarms warning of a low heart rate. Ten nurses on duty that morning could not recall hearing the beeps, which sounded at the central nurses' station, or seeing scrolling messages on three hallway signs that would have warned them as the patient's heart rate fell over the course of 20 minutes and finally stopped. State investigators said "nursing staff interviewed on the patient care unit said they were experiencing alarm fatigue and a desensitization to alarms after hearing them constantly throughout the workday." Investigators did not say why the crisis alarm was off. ... On a 15-bed unit at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, staff documented an average of 942 alarms per day - about 1 critical alarm every 90 seconds. ... The Globe, with the help of ECRI, reviewed copies of 216 reports that device manufacturers filed with the FDA on deaths in which problems with monitor alarms occurred.

cbs2011.title: Report: Mass. General Settles 'Alarm Fatigue' Death Lawsuit (CBS Boston)
cbs2011.author: CBS Boston
cbs2011.quote: BOSTON (CBS) - Massachusetts General Hospital has settled a lawsuit with the family of an 89-year-old man who died in January of 2010, when nurses did not answer the call to an alarm on the man's cardiac monitor. The settlement was reached last May, according to the Boston Globe. However, those involved have not discussed the settlement until now. The family settled for $850,000.
supports: settlement reached in May 2011, reported 28 November 2011
cbs2011.note: Cbsnews.com returns HTTP 406 to a plain client; page read through a rendering fetch, which shows the 28 November 2011 publication date, the 89-year-old man, January 2010, 'last May' for the settlement and the $850,000 figure. Ten nurses on duty could not recall hearing the beeps at the nurses' station or seeing scrolling ticker-style messages on three hallway signs that would have warned them as his heart slowed and finally stopped over a 20-minute span.'

unverified: That alarm management became National Patient Safety Goal NPSG.06.01.01 binding on accredited US hospitals from 2014. A Europe PMC search confirms the goal exists and that Joint Commission Perspectives ran 'New R3 Report addresses NPSG.06.01.01' in 2014, but the Joint Commission's own standards PDFs returned HTTP 403 and no phase-in dates were read first-hand. Kept out of the prose and off the cards.

That ECRI ranked alarm hazards its #1 health technology hazard for four consecutive years. SEA 50 says only that clinical alarm conditions 'consistently appear as the first or second most critical hazard'; the ECRI Top 10 PDFs were not reachable.
The exact date in January 2010 of the Massachusetts General Hospital death, and the patient's name. Neither appears in any source opened.
Why the crisis alarm on that monitor was switched off. The Boston Globe states explicitly that investigators did not say.

Which unit the Massachusetts General Hospital patient was on. No source opened names it - the Boston Globe says only 'the patient care unit' and 'his cardiac monitor'. The prose said 'on a cardiac ward' and the phrase has been removed; card c1's 'cardiac-ward death' likewise.

Liz Kowalczyk's assignment or motive for the investigation. The Feb 2011 article says the Globe enlisted ECRI to analyse the FDA database, and that the MGH case 'became widely known after the Globe reported on it last year' (2010) - i.e. before the series. Card c1's earlier claims that she 'was not reporting on hospital technology', 'was chasing one death' and 'spent months', and that the case 'only became a national story because' of the series, are unsourced and removed.

That a louder alarm was never the recommended fix. SEA 50 recommendation 8 does ask hospitals to assess whether critical alarm signals are audible, and 'alarm signals not audible in all areas' is one of its four counted contributing factors (25). Card c4's 'the recommended fix was never a louder speaker' is removed.
